freelance.headline: Turning ideas into
freelance.subhead: PCB design, embedded firmware and CAD for prototypes and small-batch products. I design and validate boards for a remote laboratory at IISc, and have recently started taking on freelance work. As I'm new to freelancing, I take on a small number of projects at a time and I'm upfront about what I can and can't do yet.

copy.services_title: What I can build for you
copy.services_sub: The areas I have hands-on experience in. I'm new to freelancing, so I'd rather start with something small and clearly defined, and I'll tell you honestly if a request is beyond my experience.
copy.cta_text: Describe the problem and I'll suggest an approach and a rough plan, or tell you if it isn't a good fit for me.
copy.process_sub: Simple and transparent, with review points so you can see progress and change direction early.
copy.contact_text: Boards, firmware, enclosures or the whole prototype. Tell me what you have in mind and I'll get back to you with questions, an honest view of whether I'm the right fit, and a rough plan. As a new freelancer I'm best suited to small, well-defined first projects.

services.title: Complete prototypes
services.text: Circuit, PCB, firmware and enclosure designed together, for student projects, startups and small-batch products. For a first project together, I suggest starting with one well-defined part.

process.title: Share your idea
process.text: Tell me what it should do, where it will be used and any constraints. A sketch or a reference product is enough to start.

process.title: Plan & scope
process.text: I suggest an approach, the main parts and a realistic timeline (not an optimistic one), and flag anything risky or outside my experience before we agree on scope.

process.title: Design & build
process.text: Schematic, PCB, firmware and CAD, with review points along the way. Prototypes rarely work perfectly first time, so we agree upfront how fixes and revisions are handled.

process.title: Test & hand over
process.text: Bench testing against the agreed requirements, then the agreed deliverables and documentation are handed over.

faq.a: No. This is a new, one-person freelance practice. I have professional design experience, but only a small freelance track record so far, and I'd rather tell you that now than promise too much. So I start with small, clearly defined pieces of work, give realistic estimates, keep you updated as I go, and tell you early if something isn't going to work.

I graduated in 2025 (B.E., ECE) and have about three years of hands-on product work: R&D on a smart walking stick at Yosi Innovation, and PCB design for a remote laboratory at IISc. I'm strongest in PCB design, ESP32/AVR firmware and SolidWorks, and I'm deepening my multi-layer layout and power electronics. If a project needs specialist depth, such as high-speed, RF or high-voltage design, I'll say so upfront.

faq.q: What kind of projects suit you best?
faq.a: Prototypes and small-batch products: custom boards, firmware for sensors, motors and connected devices, enclosures and mechanisms, or the whole prototype.

faq.q: Can you keep my design confidential?
faq.a: Yes. Most of my professional work is confidential, so keeping client designs private is normal for me. We can put an NDA in place before you share details.

faq.q: What do I get at the end?
faq.a: The deliverables we agree on at the start: for example a working prototype, design files and documentation. Terms are settled before any work begins, and I won't commit to anything I'm not confident I can deliver.
Bengaluru, India. Working remotely is fine, and in-person meetings are possible around Bengaluru.

projects.title: SANA: offline AI voice assistant
projects.summary: A JARVIS-style personal assistant that runs entirely on a local PC: a local language model, on-device speech recognition and synthesis, long-term memory, an animated desktop orb, and control of ESP32 hardware.
highlights: 22 skills: app and media control, file search, reminders and notes, an exact calculator, web search, and shell commands that run only after approval.
Hands-free wake-word mode with faster-whisper speech-to-text and Piper text-to-speech, all on-device.
Switches ESP32 devices and reads their sensors over MQTT.
Swappable model providers (local Ollama by default) and a strict offline mode.
Transparent animated 'universe' orb that shows when it is listening, thinking and speaking.

story.heading: Why build it
story.text: I wanted an assistant that keeps my data on my own machine and can talk to my own hardware. The language model, speech recognition, text-to-speech and memory all run locally; only the optional web tools touch the internet, and offline mode removes them.

story.heading: How it works
story.text: A wake-word listener with voice-activity detection feeds faster-whisper for speech-to-text. An agent loop passes the request to a local model through Ollama, which can call 22 skills; tool arguments are validated and repaired before anything runs. Piper speaks the answer, and SQLite stores long-term memory, reminders and notes.

story.heading: Talking to hardware
story.text: SANA switches ESP32 devices and reads their sensors over MQTT, with a mock mode until a real device is connected. Shell commands only run after I approve the exact command.

story.heading: Choosing the model
story.text: On a CPU-only i5 laptop, a 4B instruct model handled all 9 of my test tasks. A 3B model was about twice as fast but invented results on 2 tasks instead of using its tools. Hardware settings live in one config file, so adding a GPU or a separate server needs no code changes.

story.heading: What's next
story.text: A trained wake-word model, vision through a local model once a GPU is added, a phone client, and a multi-node ESP32 network.

projects.title: SculptForge: photos to printable sculptures
projects.summary: A browser app that fits template meshes to a photo and exports a closed, 3D-printable solid as STL or OBJ.
highlights: Portrait bust templates built procedurally from CC0 MakeHuman meshes (age, sex, muscle and weight targets).
Ten object templates (vase, bottle, bowl, mug, goblet and more) generated in code.
Face detection and model inference run in the browser.
Generates a watertight print solid and exports STL or OBJ.

story.heading: The idea
story.text: Turn a photo into a sculpture you can 3D print, without leaving the browser.

story.heading: Templates
story.text: Portrait busts are built from scratch by a script that downloads the CC0 MakeHuman base mesh and its age, sex, muscle and weight targets, shapes each body, smooths it, cuts out the bust and caps it into a closed solid. Object templates such as vases, bottles and mugs are generated in code.

story.heading: Fitting a photo
story.text: Face detection and model inference run in the browser. Each template is matched against the photo, and models below the match threshold are shown in red instead of being silently dropped.

story.heading: Output
story.text: The fitted mesh becomes a watertight print solid and exports as STL or OBJ, ready for a slicer.

projects.title: Freeform sculpting in SolidWorks
projects.summary: A human head sculpted in SolidWorks with the Power Surfacing add-in. Alongside my mechanical work, I practise freeform, organic modelling like this to design shapes that standard sketch-and-feature CAD can't produce, and to keep learning new techniques in SolidWorks.
highlights: Organic head form sculpted inside SolidWorks with the Power Surfacing add-in.
Subdivision-style freeform modelling, a different way of working from sketch-and-extrude parts.
Part of my ongoing self-learning in surfacing and sculpting for product design.

story.heading: Why sculpt in a mechanical CAD tool
story.text: Most of my CAD work is plates, brackets and enclosures. Products that people hold or look at also need organic shapes, so I practise freeform sculpting in SolidWorks to be able to design those too.

story.heading: The approach
story.text: The head was sculpted with Power Surfacing, an add-in that brings subdivision-style freeform modelling into SolidWorks, so the result lives in the same tool as the rest of a design.

story.heading: What's next
story.text: Applying the same techniques to product forms such as grips, handles and enclosures, where a shape has to feel right as well as work.

projects.title: Jwala: motion-control firmware
projects.summary: A clean-room motion-control firmware I'm writing from scratch, aiming at Marlin-class features: its own stepper drivers and a hardware abstraction layer for several microcontrollers, starting with the ESP32. Currently in an early development phase.
highlights: Own A4988 stepper driver and a HAL designed for multiple MCUs (ESP32 first, AVR planned).
Bare-metal ESP32 timer and GPIO layer built directly from the ESP32 Technical Reference Manual and the Xtensa ISA.
Phase 0: a build-verified level-4 interrupt stepper ISR written in Xtensa assembly.
Documented failure analysis of V1, a decision log and a bench-check tracker. A feature only counts as done once it is verified on hardware.
Roadmap toward a motion planner, G-code, homing, thermal control, bed levelling and multiple kinematics.

story.heading: Why build it
story.text: Marlin is the reference firmware for 3D printers and CNC machines, but it is a huge codebase. I wanted to understand motion control from the ground up, so Jwala is clean-room: Marlin is only the benchmark for features and behaviour, and none of its code is used.

story.heading: How it is built
story.text: A hardware abstraction layer keeps the motion code independent of the microcontroller. The ESP32 is the first target, with AVR planned. The A4988 stepper driver is my own, and the ESP32 timer and GPIO layer is written directly against the ESP32 Technical Reference Manual and the Xtensa ISA manual.

story.heading: What went wrong in V1
story.text: Version 1 compiled but did not run reliably: the bare-metal timer and interrupt layer conflicted with the ESP32 runtime. Before changing anything I wrote a full failure analysis, with evidence and a fix for every bug, and started a decision log and a bench-check tracker.

story.heading: What's next
story.text: Phase 0 rebuilds the GPIO and timer layer and moves step generation into a level-4 interrupt written in Xtensa assembly, already build-verified. The goal is one motor moving reliably, verified on the bench, before the planner, G-code, homing and thermal control.

hero_stat.label: assembly stepper interrupt, written from scratch

projects.title: Fish vending machine: mechanical design
projects.summary: A four-chamber vending machine designed in SolidWorks and built from laser-cut acrylic, with a servo-driven dispensing mechanism, a hinged lid and full fabrication documentation.
highlights: Complete SolidWorks assembly, sub-assemblies and drawing (558.8 × 158.8 × 609.6 mm overall).
DXF profiles for 3 mm acrylic laser cutting.
MG995 servo-driven dispenser caps on hinges, with servo brackets and a drive shaft.
Bill of materials, fastener-to-function map and a step-by-step assembly guide.

story.heading: The brief
story.text: A machine that stores and dispenses product from four separate chambers, built from materials that can be laser cut quickly.

story.heading: The design
story.text: Every structural part is a 3 mm acrylic plate, so the whole machine goes from SolidWorks straight to DXF cutting files. Each chamber has a hinged dispenser cap opened by an MG995 servo through a servo shaft, and a hinged lid closes the top. The machine is 558.8 × 158.8 × 609.6 mm overall, with 101.6 × 101.6 × 233.2 mm chambers.

story.heading: Documentation
story.text: The design ships with a bill of materials, a fastener-to-function map (M3 for the chambers, M6 for the hinges and lid, M1.6 at the servo joints), the assembly hierarchy, step-by-step assembly instructions and a troubleshooting guide.

story.heading: Lesson learned
story.text: The hinge model I downloaded was 40 mm with 6.5 mm holes, while the standard hinge is 38 mm with smaller holes. Downloaded models now get checked against the real part before they go into a design.

projects.title: Solar backup charging for electric vehicles (MPPT)
projects.summary: Final-year project: an on-board solar charging system that gives an electric vehicle enough backup range to reach a charging point. Covers the MPPT charge controller, the synchronous buck power stage and its firmware.
highlights: Synchronous buck converter sized from first principles (component design worksheet).
ESP32 MCPWM complementary gate drive at 48 kHz with configurable dead time.
Three iterations of the MPPT algorithm, with current sensing (ACS712) and voltage sensing.
Grew out of a mini-project on pulse generation and timing for an EV charger.

story.heading: The problem
story.text: An electric vehicle that runs out of charge away from a charging point is stuck. This project adds an on-board solar charging system so the vehicle has enough backup range to reach a charger.

story.heading: Power stage
story.text: A synchronous buck converter sits between the panel and the battery. Its component values were worked out from first principles in a design worksheet.

story.heading: Control
story.text: The ESP32's MCPWM peripheral drives the high- and low-side MOSFETs with complementary 48 kHz PWM and hardware dead time. The MPPT algorithm went through three iterations, using current sensing (ACS712) and voltage sensing to track the panel's maximum power point.

story.heading: Where it started
story.text: It grew out of a mini-project on pulse generation and timers for an EV charger.

hero_stat.label: complementary gate drive with hardware dead time
